paper_metadata.title: Llm-Tikg: Threat Intelligence Knowledge Graph Construction Utilizing Large Language Model

evidence.excerpt: Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4671345

paper_metadata.abstract: Open-source threat intelligence is often unstructured and cannot be directly applied to detection and defense. Existing knowledge-graph construction methods are limited by domain-specific entity attributes, lengthy-text analysis, large labeled-data requirements, the lack of authoritative annotated threat-intelligence datasets, and neglect of textual attack-behavior descriptions. LLM-TIKG uses GPT few-shot learning for data annotation and augmentation, creates datasets for fine-tuning a smaller 7B model, and uses the fine-tuned model for topic classification, entity and relationship extraction, and TTP extraction from attack descriptions. The resulting threat-intelligence knowledge graph supports automated analysis of textualized threat intelligence. The reported precision is 87.88% for named entity recognition and 96.53% for TTP classification.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses automated construction of a threat-intelligence knowledge graph from unstructured open-source cyber-threat reports. It targets fragmented IoC extraction, domain-specific and ambiguous entity recognition, limited handling of long reports, expensive manual annotation, and the omission of attack-behavior descriptions and MITRE ATT&CK TTP information needed for attack-chain analysis, intrusion detection, and attribution.

methodology.description: LLM-TIKG is a multi-stage pipeline. First, web crawlers collect report title, link, and cleaned content from security-company platforms, security news, and personal security blogs. GPT-3.5-turbo is prompted with task instructions, demonstrations, and report text to generate labels for topic classification, entity/relation extraction, and TTP classification. For entity/relation data, prompts specify entity types and output examples; filtering rules remove unsupported entity types, keep only relations whose endpoints are extracted entities, and manually correct part of the generated labels. TTP data combines MITRE ATT&CK malware-behavior examples with Tram data and is augmented by back-translation and GPT rewriting. Llama2-7B is instruction-tuned with LoRA on instruction/input/output examples. At inference, the model classifies reports using title and first-paragraph content, skips non-threat reports, extracts end-of-report IoCs with regular expressions and connects them to the report's main object, processes reports section by section, extracts entities and relations, and classifies TTPs sentence by sentence for reports centered on malware or attackers. Post-processing resolves generic references to preceding entities, attaches the report's main object to reduce cross-instance ambiguity, merges malware aliases with rules, clusters attack types and relationships using embeddings, cosine distance, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering, and stores the resulting graph in Neo4j.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The method uses a task-defined schema with entity categories Malware, Threat Type, Attacker, Technique, Tool, Vulnerability, IP, Domain, URL, File, and Hash, plus prompted relationship tuples. TTP classification is grounded in the MITRE ATT&CK technique and sub-technique taxonomy; the experiment reports 229 technique categories and 595 sub-technique categories represented in the dataset. The paper does not describe a separate formal KG ontology.

input_output.input_type: Unstructured English open-source cyber-threat-intelligence reports, including security-company content, security news, and personal security blogs; reports may contain prose, IoC lists, and tables.
input_output.input_granularity: Report-level topic classification uses the title and first paragraph; entity and relationship extraction is performed section by section, with overlong sections split to satisfy model input limits; TTP classification uses individual sentences; end-of-report IoCs are processed separately.
input_output.output_representation: Typed entity nodes and directed relationship edges represented as entity-relation-entity tuples, including IoCs, malware, attackers, tools, files, vulnerabilities, threat types, and MITRE ATT&CK TTP nodes; the final graph is deposited in Neo4j.

models_and_tools: GPT-3.5-turbo for few-shot annotation, data augmentation, and rewriting
Llama2-7B with LoRA instruction tuning for topic classification, entity/relation extraction, and TTP classification
GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 out-of-the-box comparison models
Word embeddings, cosine similarity, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering for consolidation
datasets: 12,545 collected blog, news, and security-analysis contents (the real-data experiment later reports 12,542 articles)
Entity and relationship extraction datasets: 1,600 manually modified instances and 15,000 coarsely filtered instances
MITRE ATT&CK malware examples and technique/sub-technique labels

evaluation.setting: Task-level evaluation covers NER, TTP classification, fine-tuning dataset quality, and training epochs, followed by application to the complete collected corpus. NER models use the same test set; BERT-CRF is trained for 20 epochs. Llama2 fine-tuning uses Python 3.9, two RTX 3090 GPUs, maximum learning rate 1×10^-4, up to 10 epochs, maximum sequence length 1024 for entity/relation extraction and 512 for the other tasks. The TTP dataset is split 10:1 into training and test sets and includes negative samples. The real-data run classifies reports and constructs a Neo4j graph.

value: NER: BERT-CRF achieved 70.98 precision, 66.40 recall, and 68.61 F1; GPT-3.5 achieved 77.83/95.72/85.85; GPT-4 achieved 79.30/94.73/86.33; LLaMA-15000 achieved 68.72/77.78/72.97; LLaMA-1600 achieved 87.88/83.99/85.89 for precision/recall/F1.
TTP technique classification: LLaMA-Tec achieved 97.47 accuracy, 96.53 precision, 99.95 recall, and 98.21 F1; TTPDrill achieved 10.23/8.17/52.15/11.05 and Tram 23.83/23.07/99.49/37.45.
TTP sub-technique classification: LLaMA-SubTec achieved 83.60 accuracy, 77.89 precision, 99.80 recall, and 87.50 F1.
On the real corpus, 9,681 of 12,542 articles were classified as threat-intelligence reports, yielding 50,745 entities and 64,948 relationships in Neo4j.

The manually corrected 1,600-example dataset produced substantially better NER precision than the 15,000-example coarsely filtered dataset, supporting the paper's observation that label quality mattered more than raw dataset size in this experiment.
The authors report that performance improved with training epochs until saturation, after which fluctuations and decline occurred.

value: Author claim: the pipeline integrates low-level IoCs with higher-level attackers, malware, tools, relationships, and TTPs.
Author claim: GPT-based few-shot annotation and augmentation reduces the manual effort required to create task datasets.
Experimental result: manually corrected data substantially improves NER precision over the larger coarsely filtered dataset.
Experimental result: the fine-tuned model reports high task-level TTP classification scores and produces a large graph from real reports.

Review-level interpretation: the section-wise extraction, report-object anchoring, alias fusion, and relationship clustering address several practical cross-sentence and cross-report integration problems.

Author-reported weakness: GPT-3.5 may hallucinate unsupported entity types and misclassify security organizations or words containing IP/Domain; filtering and manual correction are required.
Author-reported weakness: relationship extraction can interleave relationships when shared tools occur across multiple malware instances, creating ambiguity.

Review-level interpretation: graph construction is evaluated mainly through component-level NER/TTP metrics and graph counts; the paper does not report end-to-end precision, recall, or correctness of the final graph.
Review-level interpretation: the described pipeline uses alias rules and clustering, but does not report a dedicated coreference or canonical entity-linking evaluation.

value: Long reports and tabular or list-like content remain difficult for the extractor and can cause omissions.
Unsupported or incorrectly typed entities can still arise from generative annotation and require filtering or manual correction.
Shared tools and generic mentions can produce ambiguous relationship assignments across malware or attacker instances.
Data redundancy and inconsistent malware naming still require heuristic fusion and clustering.
Review-level inference: the paper leaves unresolved whether strong component-level scores translate into a correct, complete, and trustworthy end-to-end threat-intelligence graph.
Review-level inference: the paper does not establish robust cross-source entity linking, coreference resolution, or graph-update accuracy through dedicated evaluation.
